claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The fcc phase is soft and ductile, whereas the B2 or ordered phase is hard.
Dislocations pile up at internal phase boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Interfacial dislocation pile-ups create local stress concentrations that cause early microcracking and catastrophic brittle tensile failure.
Phase-selective recrystallization can fully recrystallize the soft phase while retaining a skeleton or framework of the hard phase.
In the proposed alloy, the selectively recrystallized soft phase can specifically be identified as fcc while the retained hard framework can be B2.
The treatment replaces formerly coarse fcc lamellae with fine, fully recrystallized grains.
The recrystallized soft-phase grains can accommodate strain while the retained hard-phase framework provides reinforcement.
Selective recrystallization creates new, homogeneous grain boundaries that better accommodate plastic deformation.
Selective recrystallization reduces localized dislocation accumulation at fcc/B2 interfaces.
Reduced interfacial dislocation accumulation lowers local stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation during room-temperature tension.
The retained hard-phase framework sustains or enhances the alloy's strength after selective recrystallization.
Phase-selective recrystallization will markedly increase uniform elongation relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will maintain or increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted benefits apply under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading.
The benefits require a processing window that preserves the dual-phase lamellar architecture.
Annealing temperatures, durations, or operating conditions outside the proposed processing window may produce different outcomes.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows strength merely to be maintained, but the falsification rule can be read as refuting the hypothesis when strength shows no improvement. Strength equal to the untreated baseline would therefore satisfy the prediction while potentially triggering falsification.
